name: Create and run a RuntimeClass
objective: CKS › Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities. Drill EVERY RuntimeClass corner harder than the exam: create a class and its required handler, the optional scheduling/overhead fields, select it per-pod and per-Deployment, contrast with the default runtime, layer securityContext hardening on top, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Create a RuntimeClass
questions.teach:
A **RuntimeClass** (`apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1`, `kind: RuntimeClass`) is a **cluster-scoped** object naming a container runtime the kubelet can use. Its one required field, **`handler`**, is a string the node's CRI maps to a runtime binary — e.g. gVisor's `runsc`.

**Gotcha:** `handler` is a **top-level** field, NOT under `spec` — RuntimeClass has no `spec`.
questions.prompt:
Create a cluster-scoped RuntimeClass named `gvisor` whose `handler` is `runsc`.

Target: `kubectl get runtimeclass gvisor` exists and its `.handler` is exactly `runsc`.
questions.hint: `apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1`, `kind: RuntimeClass`, `metadata.name: gvisor`, and a top-level `handler: runsc` (NOT under spec). `kubectl apply -f -`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc
YAML
questions.eli5:
Normally your containers all run on the same engine on a node (usually `runc`), and they share the machine's one Linux kernel. That's fast, but it means a nasty container that breaks out could reach the whole host. For risky workloads you'd rather run them in something more **isolated**, like a mini-sandbox.

A **RuntimeClass** is how you give Kubernetes a *menu of engines* to choose from. Think of it like picking a shipping option at checkout: "standard" (the default runtime) vs "armoured truck" (a sandbox like gVisor). You create a named option, and later pods say which one they want.

A RuntimeClass is a **cluster-wide** object (not tied to a namespace). It has one job: carry a **`handler`** — a short name the node's container runtime already knows how to map to an actual sandbox binary. For gVisor that handler is **`runsc`**. So you create a RuntimeClass called `gvisor` whose `handler` is `runsc`.

The one thing people trip on: unlike almost every other Kubernetes object, **`handler` is a top-level field — RuntimeClass has NO `spec:`.** You write `handler: runsc` right under `metadata`, not nested inside a `spec`.

**Watch out for:**

- `handler` is a **top-level** field, **NOT** under `spec:` — RuntimeClass has no `spec` at all.
- Use the right `apiVersion` and `kind`: `node.k8s.io/v1`, `kind: RuntimeClass`.
- RuntimeClass is **cluster-scoped** — no namespace; `kubectl get runtimeclass` (not `-n ...`).
- The `handler` string must match what the node's CRI is configured for (gVisor = `runsc`); a made-up handler won't resolve at run time.
- Creating the class doesn't install the runtime — it just names a handler the node is expected to have.
questions.deepDive:
## Creating a RuntimeClass — full rundown

### Mental model
A **RuntimeClass** is a cluster-scoped object that names a **container runtime handler** the kubelet/CRI can select on a per-pod basis. It decouples "which isolation mechanism" from the workload: operators define classes (e.g. `gvisor` → `runsc`, `kata` → `kata`), workloads opt in by name. The default runtime (usually `runc`) shares the host kernel directly; **sandboxed** runtimes (gVisor, Kata) interpose an extra boundary so a container escape doesn't immediately reach the host kernel — the core CKS reason to use them.

### The object
```yaml
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1      # stable since 1.20
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor                  # the name pods reference via runtimeClassName
handler: runsc                  # TOP-LEVEL — the CRI handler string
```

### Field layout (the big gotcha)
RuntimeClass has **no `spec`**. Its fields sit at the top level next to `metadata`:

| Field | Level | Required | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `handler` | top-level | ✅ | CRI handler name → runtime binary |
| `scheduling` | top-level | optional | nodeSelector/tolerations to steer pods to capable nodes |
| `overhead` | top-level | optional | per-pod resource overhead the sandbox consumes |

### How `handler` resolves
The handler is a **string the node's CRI is pre-configured to understand**. For containerd, `/etc/containerd/config.toml` maps a runtime handler name to a binary:
```toml
[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runsc]
  runtime_type = "io.containerd.runsc.v1"
```
So RuntimeClass `handler: runsc` ↔ containerd's `runtimes.runsc` ↔ the gVisor `runsc` binary. If the node has no such handler, pods using the class fail to start with a runtime error.

### Common handlers
| RuntimeClass handler | Runtime | Isolation model |
|---|---|---|
| `runc` (default, no class) | standard OCI | shared host kernel |
| `runsc` | gVisor | user-space kernel (ptrace/KVM) intercepts syscalls |
| `kata` | Kata Containers | lightweight VM per pod |

### Commands
```bash
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc
YAML

kubectl get runtimeclass                      # cluster-scoped list
kubectl get runtimeclass gvisor -o jsonpath='{.handler}'; echo   # -> runsc
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`handler` is top-level, not under `spec`.** RuntimeClass has no `spec` — the #1 mistake. YAML with `spec: { handler: ... }` is rejected/ignored.
- **Cluster-scoped.** No namespace; `kubectl get runtimeclass`, never `-n`.
- **`apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1`**, `kind: RuntimeClass` — not `v1`/`apps/v1`.
- Creating the class **does not install** gVisor/Kata — it only references a handler the node must already provide. A pod using a class whose handler is absent on the node stays Pending / fails to start ("RuntimeHandler not found").
- The class **name** (what pods reference) and the **handler** (CRI binary key) are distinct — they often differ (`gvisor` → `runsc`).

### Quick reference
```yaml
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc        # top-level; NO spec:
```
```bash
kubectl get runtimeclass gvisor -o jsonpath='{.handler}'   # runsc
```

questions.title: A RuntimeClass with scheduling + overhead
questions.teach:
A RuntimeClass can carry optional fields the scheduler honours: **`scheduling.nodeSelector`** steers its pods onto nodes that actually have the runtime, and **`overhead.podFixed`** reserves resources the sandbox itself consumes. Both sit alongside the top-level `handler`.

**Gotcha:** `scheduling` and `overhead` are **top-level** on the RuntimeClass (siblings of `handler`), not inside a pod spec.
questions.prompt:
Create a RuntimeClass named `kata` with:
- `handler` = `kata`
- `scheduling.nodeSelector` = `{ runtime: kata }`
- `overhead.podFixed` = `{ memory: 64Mi, cpu: 50m }`

Target: `kata` has handler `kata`, that nodeSelector, and that podFixed overhead.
questions.hint: All three are top-level fields on the RuntimeClass object: `handler:`, `scheduling: { nodeSelector: {...} }`, `overhead: { podFixed: {...} }`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: kata
handler: kata
scheduling:
  nodeSelector:
    runtime: kata
overhead:
  podFixed:
    memory: 64Mi
    cpu: 50m
YAML

verification.description: RuntimeClass 'kata': handler kata + scheduling.nodeSelector runtime=kata + overhead.podFixed mem 64Mi/cpu 50m

questions.eli5:
A basic RuntimeClass just says "use this engine." But a sandbox engine often isn't installed on *every* node, and it also eats some extra resources just to exist. A RuntimeClass can carry two optional bits of helpful info to deal with both.

Imagine the sandbox runtime is a special printer that only exists in **one room** of the office, and it needs its own desk space:

- **`scheduling.nodeSelector`** is a note that says "pods using this class can only go to rooms that have the printer." Here, `{ runtime: kata }` means "only schedule me onto nodes labelled `runtime=kata`." This stops a pod from landing on a node that can't actually run the sandbox.
- **`overhead.podFixed`** is reserving the desk space the printer itself takes up — the sandbox engine always consumes some CPU and memory before your app uses any. `{ memory: 64Mi, cpu: 50m }` tells the scheduler "count an extra 64Mi/50m against this pod" so nodes don't get overbooked.

Both of these are **top-level** fields on the RuntimeClass, sitting right next to `handler` — they are *not* things you put inside a pod.

**Watch out for:**

- `scheduling` and `overhead` are **top-level on the RuntimeClass** (siblings of `handler`), **not** inside a pod spec.
- Still no `spec:` — everything hangs off the top level.
- `scheduling.nodeSelector` makes pods of this class only land on **matching, labelled** nodes; mislabel the node and pods go Pending.
- `overhead.podFixed` adds to the pod's effective resource request — it's charged on top of your containers' requests.
- Resource quantities use Kubernetes units: `64Mi` (mebibytes), `50m` (millicores) — spell them exactly.
- These are optional; `handler` alone is a valid RuntimeClass.
questions.deepDive:
## RuntimeClass scheduling & overhead — full rundown

### Mental model
A sandboxed runtime is usually **not present on every node** and **consumes resources** just to run the sandbox. The optional `scheduling` and `overhead` fields on a RuntimeClass let the operator encode both facts *once, on the class*, so every pod that picks the class is automatically steered to capable nodes and accounted for correctly — without each pod author repeating it.

### The two optional fields (both top-level)
```yaml
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: kata
handler: kata
scheduling:
  nodeSelector:
    runtime: kata          # pods of this class only schedule onto nodes with runtime=kata
  # tolerations:           # optional: also tolerate taints those nodes carry
  # - key: runtime
  #   operator: Equal
  #   value: kata
  #   effect: NoSchedule
overhead:
  podFixed:
    memory: 64Mi           # resources the sandbox itself consumes
    cpu: 50m
```

| Field | Effect |
|---|---|
| `scheduling.nodeSelector` | **merged into** every pod's nodeSelector by the RuntimeClass admission controller; pod only lands on matching nodes |
| `scheduling.tolerations` | added to the pod so it tolerates taints on the runtime-capable nodes |
| `overhead.podFixed` | added to the pod's effective resource requests/limits for scheduling and eviction accounting |

### How `scheduling` works
The RuntimeClass admission controller **injects** the class's `nodeSelector`/`tolerations` into any pod that references the class. If the pod already has conflicting nodeSelector keys, admission **rejects** the pod (conflict), rather than silently merging. This guarantees sandboxed pods can't be scheduled onto nodes lacking the runtime.

### How `overhead` works (Pod Overhead)
`overhead.podFixed` is added on top of the sum of container requests when the scheduler decides fit, and counted by the kubelet for cgroup sizing and eviction. It models the fixed cost of the sandbox (e.g. the Kata VM, the gVisor sentry). It does **not** run any container — it is pure bookkeeping so a node isn't overcommitted.

Effective pod request ≈ Σ(container requests) + `overhead.podFixed`.

### Resource unit reference
| Unit | Means |
|---|---|
| `50m` | 0.05 CPU (millicores) |
| `64Mi` | 64 mebibytes (2^20 bytes) |
| `64M` | 64 megabytes (10^6) — different from `Mi` |

### Commands
```bash
kubectl apply -f kata-rc.yaml
kubectl get runtimeclass kata -o jsonpath='{.scheduling.nodeSelector}'; echo
kubectl get runtimeclass kata -o jsonpath='{.overhead.podFixed}'; echo
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`scheduling` and `overhead` are top-level on the RuntimeClass**, siblings of `handler` — never inside pod spec. (RuntimeClass still has no `spec`.)
- `scheduling.nodeSelector` is **injected into pods**; a pod that already sets a **conflicting** nodeSelector key is **rejected** by admission.
- Label the capable nodes to match (`kubectl label node <n> runtime=kata`) or pods of this class go **Pending** (no matching node).
- `overhead.podFixed` **adds to** resource requests — forgetting it can let nodes become overcommitted; setting it too high wastes capacity.
- Mind units: `Mi` ≠ `M`, `m` is millicores. `cpu: 50m` is 0.05 CPU, not 50.
- Both fields are optional; omit them for a minimal class (just `handler`).

### Quick reference
```yaml
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata: { name: kata }
handler: kata
scheduling:
  nodeSelector: { runtime: kata }
overhead:
  podFixed: { memory: 64Mi, cpu: 50m }
```
```bash
kubectl get runtimeclass kata -o jsonpath='{.handler}{" "}{.scheduling.nodeSelector}{" "}{.overhead.podFixed}'; echo
```

questions.title: Run a pod on a RuntimeClass
questions.teach:
A pod opts into a RuntimeClass via **`spec.runtimeClassName: <name>`** — a pod-level field. `kubectl run` has no flag for it, so inject it with `--overrides='{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":"gvisor"}}'`, or just write the YAML.

**Gotcha:** since `runsc` isn't installed here the pod won't actually run on gVisor — we grade only that `.spec.runtimeClassName` is set, not the phase.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `runtimeclass-learn`, create pod `sandboxed` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) requesting the `gvisor` RuntimeClass via `spec.runtimeClassName`.

Target: pod `sandboxed` has `.spec.runtimeClassName` = `gvisor`.
questions.hint: `kubectl run sandboxed -n runtimeclass-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --overrides='{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":"gvisor"}}' --command -- sleep 3600`, or apply YAML with `spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: sandboxed, namespace: runtimeclass-learn }
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
YAML
questions.eli5:
You've created the "sandbox" option (the `gvisor` RuntimeClass). Now you actually order it for a specific pod. A pod chooses its runtime with one line: **`spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor`**. That's the pod raising its hand and saying "run me on the gvisor engine, please."

The little annoyance: the quick `kubectl run` command has **no flag** for this. There's `--image`, there's `--command`, but no `--runtime-class`. So you have two options: write the pod as YAML (easy, `runtimeClassName: gvisor` goes under `spec`), or squeeze it into `kubectl run` using `--overrides='{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":"gvisor"}}'`, which lets you hand-inject any extra spec fields.

One honest caveat for this lab: the real `runsc` sandbox binary isn't installed on these nodes. So the pod won't *actually* boot inside gVisor. That's fine — the grader only checks that you **set `.spec.runtimeClassName` to `gvisor`**, not that the pod reaches Running. In a real cluster with gVisor installed, it would run sandboxed.

**Watch out for:**

- The field is **`spec.runtimeClassName`** — a pod-level field (sibling of `containers`), a plain string naming the class.
- `kubectl run` has **no `--runtime-class` flag** — use `--overrides='{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":"gvisor"}}'` or write YAML.
- The name must match an **existing** RuntimeClass exactly; a typo means the pod is rejected with "RuntimeClass not found."
- Here the pod may stay **Pending / not run** because `runsc` isn't installed — expected; only the spec field is graded.
- `runtimeClassName` is **immutable** once the pod exists — to change it you delete and recreate the pod.
questions.deepDive:
## Running a pod on a RuntimeClass — full rundown

### Mental model
A RuntimeClass is only a *named option*; a pod **opts in** by setting **`spec.runtimeClassName`** to the class name. At admission, Kubernetes resolves the name to the RuntimeClass object, injects any `scheduling`/`overhead` it carries, and passes the class's `handler` to the kubelet, which tells the CRI to start the pod's containers with that runtime. No pod field names the handler directly — only the class name.

### Where the field lives
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sandboxed
  namespace: runtimeclass-learn
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor      # pod-level, sibling of containers
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
```
`runtimeClassName` is a **string** at `spec.runtimeClassName`. It is **not** per-container.

### Creating it
`kubectl run` has **no `--runtime-class` flag**, so either write YAML (above) or inject via `--overrides`:
```bash
kubectl run sandboxed -n runtimeclass-learn --image=busybox:1.36 \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":"gvisor"}}' \
  --command -- sleep 3600
```
`--overrides` deep-merges the JSON into the generated pod spec — the general trick for any field the CLI lacks a flag for.

### Verifying
```bash
kubectl -n runtimeclass-learn get pod sandboxed \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'; echo      # -> gvisor
```

### What happens at runtime
| Situation | Result |
|---|---|
| Class exists, handler present on node | pod runs under the sandbox runtime |
| Class exists, handler **absent** on node | pod fails to start / Pending ("RuntimeHandler not found") |
| Class name **doesn't exist** | pod **rejected at admission** ("RuntimeClass not found") |

In this lab `runsc` isn't installed, so the pod won't reach Running — **only `.spec.runtimeClassName == gvisor` is graded**, not the phase.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Field is `spec.runtimeClassName`** (pod-level, a bare string) — not per-container, not `runtimeClass`.
- **No `kubectl run` flag** — use `--overrides` or YAML.
- The name must reference an **existing** RuntimeClass; a non-existent name is rejected at admission, a valid-name-but-missing-handler fails at the node.
- **Immutable** once set — change requires delete + recreate (see the fix-it lab).
- Here, Pending/CreateContainerError due to missing `runsc` is **expected**; grade is the spec field.
- Don't confuse the **class name** (`gvisor`) with the **handler** (`runsc`) — the pod references the name.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl run sandboxed -n runtimeclass-learn --image=busybox:1.36 \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":"gvisor"}}' --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl -n runtimeclass-learn get pod sandboxed -o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'; echo
```

questions.title: Contrast with a default-runtime pod
questions.teach:
RuntimeClass is per-workload: sandbox the sensitive pods, leave the rest on the node's default runtime (usually `runc`), which shares the host kernel directly. A pod with **no `runtimeClassName`** uses that default.

**Gotcha:** `-o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'` returns an **empty string** for a default-runtime pod — that emptiness is the correct "normal" state, not a mistake.
questions.prompt:
In `runtimeclass-learn`, create pod `normal` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) with **no** `runtimeClassName`.

Target: `normal` exists with an empty `.spec.runtimeClassName`, while `sandboxed`'s is still `gvisor` — the two differ.
questions.hint: `kubectl run normal -n runtimeclass-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600` — no overrides. Leaving runtimeClassName unset selects the default runtime.

verification.description: 'normal' has empty runtimeClassName while 'sandboxed' has gvisor (they differ)

questions.eli5:
Not every pod needs the armoured-truck treatment. Sandboxes cost a little speed and resources, so the smart approach is: **only sandbox the sensitive pods, and leave the ordinary ones on the normal runtime.** RuntimeClass is per-pod, so you mix and match freely.

A pod that says **nothing** about `runtimeClassName` just uses the node's **default runtime** — normally `runc`, which runs the container directly on the shared host kernel. That's the fast, ordinary path. You don't write "default" anywhere; you simply **leave the field out**.

So here you make a `normal` pod with no `runtimeClassName` at all, standing next to your `sandboxed` pod which has `gvisor`. Side by side, they prove the point: same cluster, two different isolation levels, chosen per pod.

The thing that confuses people: when you ask a default pod for its runtime class with `kubectl ... -o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'`, you get back... **nothing — an empty string.** That blank is not an error or a bug; it's the *correct* way to say "this pod uses the default runtime." Emptiness is the normal state.

**Watch out for:**

- A pod with **no `runtimeClassName`** uses the node's **default runtime** (usually `runc`) — you don't type "default", you omit the field.
- `-o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'` returns an **empty string** for a default pod — that emptiness is correct, not a mistake.
- Don't add `runtimeClassName: ""` or `runtimeClassName: default` trying to "set" the default — just leave it unset.
- The point of this step is **contrast**: `normal` is empty, `sandboxed` is `gvisor` — they must differ.
- The default runtime shares the host kernel directly (less isolation) — that's the trade-off you accept for normal pods.
questions.deepDive:
## Default-runtime pods vs RuntimeClass — full rundown

### Mental model
RuntimeClass is a **per-workload opt-in**. The design intent is selective isolation: run untrusted / high-risk workloads under a sandbox (gVisor/Kata) and leave everything else on the node's **default runtime** (`runc`), which is faster but shares the host kernel directly. A pod that omits `runtimeClassName` gets the default — that's the baseline, and its empty `runtimeClassName` is the normal, correct state.

### The default runtime
- Set at the **node/CRI** level (e.g. containerd's `default_runtime_name = "runc"`).
- A pod with **no** `spec.runtimeClassName` uses it — no field, no admission injection, no overhead.
- `runc` runs containers as normal host processes isolated only by namespaces + cgroups (shared kernel). A kernel-level container escape reaches the host — the reason to sandbox sensitive pods.

### Isolation comparison
| | Default (`runc`, no class) | Sandboxed (`gvisor`/`kata`) |
|---|---|---|
| Kernel | shared host kernel | interposed (user-space kernel / micro-VM) |
| Overhead | lowest | higher (CPU/mem/latency) |
| Blast radius of escape | host | contained to sandbox |
| How selected | omit `runtimeClassName` | set `runtimeClassName` |

### Creating a default pod
```bash
kubectl run normal -n runtimeclass-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600
# no --overrides, no runtimeClassName
```

### The "empty string" check
```bash
kubectl -n runtimeclass-learn get pod normal     -o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'; echo   # -> (empty line)
kubectl -n runtimeclass-learn get pod sandboxed  -o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'; echo   # -> gvisor
```
An **empty result for `normal`** is expected — the field is simply absent, which means "default runtime." The two pods differ, which is the graded signal.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Omit the field for default** — do not set `runtimeClassName: ""` or `runtimeClassName: default`. There is no RuntimeClass literally named "default"; the default lives in CRI config.
- **Empty jsonpath output is correct**, not a failure — it prints a blank line for an unset field.
- RuntimeClass is **per-pod/per-template** — one cluster mixes sandboxed and default pods freely; this is the intended security posture.
- A default pod has **no injected nodeSelector/overhead** (those come only from a referenced class).
- Default `runc` shares the host kernel — layer additional hardening (seccomp, drop caps, non-root) on sensitive pods even when sandboxed.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl run normal -n runtimeclass-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600
# compare
for p in normal sandboxed; do
  echo -n "$p: "; kubectl -n runtimeclass-learn get pod $p -o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'; echo
done
# normal:            <-- empty = default runtime (correct)
# sandboxed: gvisor
```
